newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia Osiguranje reverses five years' decline.
newsitem.headline: Croatia Osiguranje reverses five years' decline.

text.p: Croatia's biggest insurance company, state-owned Croatia Osiguranje d.d., said on Tuesday it had turned around after five years of decline and recorded a 7.3 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 34.3 million kuna ($5.6 million).

The company's chief executive, Suad Rizvanbegovic, told the annual shareholders meeting that premium income in 1996 had grown for the first time since 1990, by 2.2 percent, with the small life insurance sector growing fastest.
Car insurance, which accounts for almost half the company's income, rose 0.5 percent on last year while income from life insurance rose by 54 percent.
He qualified that as a success, given the tough competition from small private companies especially in those two segments of the market.
The only sector that recorded a fall in premium income was property insurance which was 6.4 percent lower than last year.
The company said in its annual report that this was due to war damage and other economic problems related to the war in former Yugoslavia, and to restructuring of the economy.
Turnover, which was reported at 2.3 billion kuna, and operating costs both fell five percent due to a change in book-keeping procedures, Rizvanbegovic said.
Dividends rose 69 percent compared to last year.

The company will pay 112 kuna dividend per A-series issue, held by individuals, or eight percent of their nominal value. It will grant 65 kuna per B-series share, held by companies, or 4.6 percent of their value.
Both issues have a nominal price of 1,400 kuna and were traded at 1,250 kuna on the Zagreb Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
Croatia Osiguranje d.d. is 77.5 percent owned by the state while other companies hold 19.7 percent and individuals the remaining 2.8 percent.
According to the Croatian Insurance Bureau, the company had the lion's share with more than 77 percent of the domestic insurance market at the end of 1995. Data for 1996 is not yet available.
The company faces tough competition from some twenty-odd newly-founded private insurers which have flooded the market since it opened to competition after the fall of communism.
Rizvanbegovic said he expected only seven or eight to stay in business in the next few years.
"I cannot understand insurants who want to put the security of their property and lives in the hands of those instable businesses," Rizvanbegovic said.
He singled out a surplus of labour as the biggest single problem for the company and indicated that staff could be cut.
He cited the increase of premium income, the quality of services and profit as the three main goals of the company in the near future.
-- Davor Huic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075 ($ = 6.139 Croatian Kuna)
